items.prompt: Which part of a neuron typically receives incoming signals from other neurons?

options.label: Dendrites
Node of Ranvier
Myelin sheath
Axon terminal

rubric: Dendrites are the branching extensions that receive input from other cells.
Axon terminals send signals, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: What is the name of the small gap between two communicating neurons?

options.label: Axon hillock
Soma
Glial junction
Synaptic cleft

rubric: The synaptic cleft separates presynaptic and postsynaptic cells.
The axon hillock is where action potentials start, not the gap.

items.prompt: Which ion rushes into the neuron during the rising phase of an action potential?

options.label: Potassium (K+)
Calcium (Ca2+)
Chloride (Cl-)
Sodium (Na+)

rubric: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters, depolarizing the cell.
K+ leaves the cell during repolarization.

items.prompt: Which brain region is mainly responsible for coordinating balance and fine-tuning movement?

options.label: Amygdala
Cerebellum
Thalamus
Hippocampus

rubric: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
The hippocampus is linked to memory formation, a frequent confusion.

items.prompt: Which type of molecule is released by a presynaptic neuron to signal across a synapse?

options.label: Enzyme
Neurotransmitter
Hormone
Antibody

rubric: Neurotransmitters carry the signal across the synaptic cleft.
Hormones travel through blood, not across synapses.

items.prompt: Which of the following are neurotransmitters? Select all that apply.

options.label: Glutamate
Collagen
Dopamine
Hemoglobin

rubric: Dopamine and glutamate are neurotransmitters.
Hemoglobin and collagen are proteins with other roles.

items.prompt: A student studying a diagram of the brain is asked to label the lobe that processes visual information. It sits at the back of the head. Which lobe should the student label?

options.label: Occipital lobe
Frontal lobe
Temporal lobe
Parietal lobe

rubric: The occipital lobe at the back handles primary visual processing.
The temporal lobe is for hearing and memory, often confused.

items.prompt: Why does the neuron's resting membrane potential sit at about -70 mV?

options.label: The nucleus produces a steady negative charge that fills the cytoplasm
Myelin insulates the axon and traps negative charge inside the cell, holding it negative
Neurotransmitters constantly bind to the membrane and charge it negatively from outside
Unequal ion distribution and selective permeability keep the inside negative

rubric: Ion gradients plus leak channels, mostly K+, set the resting potential.
Myelin affects speed, not the resting potential.

items.prompt: What does myelin do for an axon?

options.label: Increases the size of each action potential along the axon
Stores neurotransmitters so they can be released faster
Speeds conduction by letting the signal jump between nodes
Receives signals from neighboring neurons across the synapse

rubric: Myelin enables saltatory conduction, speeding signals.
Myelin does not make action potentials larger; they are all-or-none.

items.prompt: What does it mean that an action potential is 'all-or-none'?

options.label: It travels along the axon only if every neighboring neuron also fires at once
It occurs in the whole brain at once or not at all, never in single cells
Once threshold is reached, it fires at full size whatever the stimulus strength
A stronger stimulus produces a taller action potential in the same neuron each time

rubric: Action potentials have fixed amplitude once threshold is crossed.
Stimulus strength is coded by firing rate, not amplitude.

items.prompt: How does an inhibitory neurotransmitter such as GABA mainly affect the postsynaptic neuron?

options.label: It permanently destroys the receptors on the postsynaptic cell
It makes the neuron less likely to fire an action potential
It forces the neuron to fire at a faster rate than normal
It converts the neuron's signal into a hormone-based message

rubric: Inhibitory input hyperpolarizes or stabilizes the cell, lowering firing probability.
Inhibition is not receptor destruction or excitation.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between the sensory and motor neurons?

options.label: Sensory neurons carry information toward the CNS; motor neurons carry commands away
Sensory neurons use electrical signals; motor neurons use only chemical ones
Sensory neurons carry commands to muscles; motor neurons carry information from skin
Sensory neurons exist only in the brain; motor neurons only in the spinal cord

rubric: Afferent sensory neurons go to the CNS; efferent motor neurons go out.
Reversing the direction is the common error.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe synaptic transmission at a chemical synapse? Select all that apply.

options.label: Neurotransmitter stays in the cleft permanently to keep signaling
Calcium entry triggers vesicles to release neurotransmitter
Action potentials jump directly across the cleft as electricity
Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell

rubric: Ca2+ triggers release and transmitter binds postsynaptic receptors.
Chemical synapses do not pass spikes across the gap, and transmitter is cleared or reuptaken.

items.prompt: A person touches a hot stove and pulls their hand away before feeling pain. A teacher explains this to the class. Which explanation best accounts for the quick response?

options.label: The brain predicts the touch in advance and sends a movement command before the hand reaches the stove
Pain receptors directly release hormones that move the hand within seconds
A spinal reflex arc links sensory input to motor output without waiting for the brain
The muscles sense the heat themselves and contract without any neural input

rubric: Reflex arcs route through the spinal cord for speed.
Muscles need motor neuron input; hormones are too slow.

items.prompt: Why do myelinated axons conduct action potentials faster than unmyelinated axons of the same diameter?

options.label: Myelin increases sodium flow along every part of the axon, so each patch fires sooner
Myelin carries neurotransmitter along the axon, so the signal can skip the synapse
The signal jumps between nodes of Ranvier, so depolarization is regenerated only at gaps
Myelin pumps ions out of the axon, so the resting potential becomes more positive

rubric: Myelin insulates the axon so the action potential is regenerated only at nodes (saltatory conduction).
Distractors confuse myelin with ion pumping, transmitter transport, or more sodium flow along the whole membrane.

items.prompt: What directly triggers release of neurotransmitter from an axon terminal?

options.label: Reuptake of transmitter by transporters in the terminal membrane
Entry of calcium ions through voltage-gated channels
Exit of potassium ions through leak channels in the terminal
Binding of neurotransmitter to autoreceptors on the terminal

rubric: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and Ca2+ entry causes vesicles to fuse and release transmitter.
Distractors name real processes (autoreceptors, K+ leak, reuptake) that do not trigger vesicle release.

items.prompt: A patient understands spoken sentences well but speaks in slow, effortful, halting phrases. Which region is most likely damaged?

options.label: Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe
The cerebellum at the back of the brain
Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
Primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe

rubric: Broca's area damage causes non-fluent speech production with relatively preserved comprehension.
Wernicke's damage typically impairs comprehension with fluent but meaningless speech.

items.prompt: Why does an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) make a neuron less likely to fire?

options.label: It shortens the axon's length so that fewer inputs can sum at the soma
It raises sodium permeability so the neuron cannot recover between spikes
It moves the membrane potential away from threshold, often by hyperpolarizing
It breaks down the neurotransmitter in the cleft so excitatory signals cannot arrive

rubric: IPSPs (e.g., Cl- entry or K+ exit) hold the potential further from threshold.
Distractors invent mechanisms such as transmitter destruction, higher sodium permeability, or axon changes.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the main role of the cerebellum?

options.label: Storing long-term declarative memories of past events
Generating the initial command to start a voluntary movement
Regulating heart rate and breathing through reflex centers
Coordinating the timing and smoothness of movements

rubric: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and supports motor learning.
Distractors assign motor cortex, brainstem, or hippocampal functions to it.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe action potentials in a typical neuron? Select all that apply.

options.label: Once threshold is reached, the spike has the same amplitude each time
The spike shrinks gradually as it travels down the axon
A stronger stimulus is usually signalled by a higher firing rate
A stronger stimulus produces a larger action potential

rubric: Action potentials are all-or-none and intensity is coded mainly by frequency.
Distractors treat spikes as graded or decaying, which describes graded potentials.

items.prompt: After surgery removing both hippocampi, a patient can chat normally and recall childhood events. He cannot remember meeting his doctors from one day to the next, yet he gradually improves at a mirror-drawing task he never recalls practicing. Which interpretation best fits these observations?

options.label: The hippocampus is needed to form new declarative memories, but not for old ones or motor learning
The hippocampus is needed to form all new memories, so his drawing gains must reflect conscious rehearsal he forgot
The hippocampus is needed to retrieve old declarative memories, so his childhood recall must rely on a spared backup route
The hippocampus holds long-term storage for all memory types, so old memories and skills should both have been erased

rubric: Hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia for declarative memory while skill learning uses other circuits.
Distractors treat the hippocampus as the sole site of storage, learning, or language.

items.prompt: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a threshold of -55 mV. Three EPSPs of +6 mV each and one IPSP of -2 mV arrive together and sum. What happens?

options.label: It does not fire; the potential only reaches -58 mV
It fires; the potential reaches -54 mV
It fires; the potential reaches -50 mV
It does not fire; the potential only reaches -64 mV

rubric: Net change is 18 - 2 = +16 mV, giving -54 mV, which is above threshold.
Distractors come from arithmetic or sign errors in summing inputs.

items.prompt: A neuron rests at -70 mV and the K+ equilibrium potential is about -90 mV. Extra K+ channels open. What is the most likely effect?

options.label: The membrane moves toward -90 mV, making firing less likely
The membrane moves toward 0 mV, making firing more likely
The membrane moves toward +60 mV, making firing more likely
The membrane stays at -70 mV because K+ in and out cancel

rubric: K+ flows out, pulling the potential toward its equilibrium potential and hyperpolarizing the cell.
Distractors confuse the direction of K+ flow or use the Na+ equilibrium potential.

items.prompt: A dentist injects lidocaine, which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, near a tooth's nerve. What is the most likely result?

options.label: The pain axons cannot generate action potentials, so no signal reaches the brain
Spikes still travel, but the pain cortex is silenced directly by the drug
The axons conduct normally, but their terminals release extra transmitter
The pain axons fire continuously, flooding the brain with signals

rubric: Without Na+ channel opening, the rising phase of the action potential fails and the pain signal is not conducted.
Distractors predict hyperactivity or a central site of action, which do not follow from blocking axonal Na+ channels.

items.prompt: You touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you feel pain. Which sequence best describes the reflex pathway?

options.label: Muscle, motor neuron, spinal cord, then sensory neuron
Motor neuron, spinal cord, sensory neuron, then muscle
Sensory neuron, somatosensory cortex, motor cortex, motor neuron, then muscle
Sensory neuron, spinal interneuron, motor neuron, then muscle

rubric: Spinal reflexes route sensory input through the cord to motor neurons without waiting for the cortex.
Distractors reverse the order or send the signal through the cortex first.

items.prompt: A drug blocks the presynaptic transporters that take serotonin back up from the synaptic cleft. What is the expected effect at that synapse?

options.label: Serotonin stays in the cleft longer, increasing receptor activation
Postsynaptic receptors are blocked, so serotonin has no effect
Serotonin is broken down faster, reducing receptor activation
Less serotonin is released, reducing receptor activation

rubric: Blocking reuptake leaves more transmitter in the cleft for longer.
Distractors describe reduced release, faster breakdown, or receptor blockade, none of which reuptake inhibition causes.

items.prompt: A stroke destroys the hand area of the left primary motor cortex. Which outcomes would you expect? Select all that apply.

options.label: Largely normal movement of the left hand
Speech comprehension that is typically intact
Loss of balance as the main deficit
Weakness of the left hand
Weakness of the right hand

rubric: Motor cortex controls the opposite side of the body, and the hand area does not hold language comprehension.
Distractors reverse laterality or assign a cerebellar deficit to motor cortex damage.

items.prompt: In a lab, a researcher applies curare, which blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, to a nerve-muscle preparation. She then stimulates the motor neuron and records from both the axon and the muscle. Which result should she predict?

options.label: The motor axon fires normally and the muscle contracts, but more weakly because less acetylcholine is released
The motor axon fires normally, but the muscle fibers do not depolarize or contract
The motor axon cannot fire because curare blocks its sodium channels, so no acetylcholine is released
The muscle contracts continuously because acetylcholine builds up in the synaptic cleft

rubric: Curare blocks postsynaptic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, so the axon still fires but the muscle fails to respond.
Distractors place the block in the neuron, predict overstimulation, or involve sensory neurons.

items.prompt: A neuron has a resting potential of -70 mV. Its K+ equilibrium potential is -90 mV and its Na+ equilibrium potential is +60 mV. Extra K+ leak channels open while all other channels stay as they were. Where does the membrane potential move?

options.label: Toward -90 mV, so the cell hyperpolarizes
Toward +60 mV, so the cell depolarizes
Toward 0 mV, so the channels act nonselectively
It stays at -70 mV, since K+ is at equilibrium

rubric: Opening more K+ channels pulls Vm toward E_K, which is more negative than rest, so the cell hyperpolarizes.
Distractors confuse the direction of the driving force or treat the resting potential as K+ equilibrium.

items.prompt: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a spike threshold of -55 mV. Three excitatory synapses each add a +5 mV EPSP and one inhibitory synapse adds a -2 mV IPSP, all arriving at the soma at the same instant. Assuming linear summation, what happens?

options.label: Spike fires; the membrane reaches exactly -55 mV
No spike; the membrane reaches about -63 mV
No spike; the membrane reaches about -57 mV
Spike fires; the membrane reaches about -52 mV

rubric: Net change is +15 - 2 = +13 mV, giving about -57 mV, which is below threshold.
Distractors ignore the IPSP or add the potentials incorrectly.

items.prompt: Tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, is applied to the middle of a healthy myelinated axon. What do you predict for an action potential approaching that region?

options.label: Resting potential drops to -90 mV and spikes get larger
Spikes fail to propagate; resting potential barely changes
Spikes still occur but conduct slowly, as in demyelination
Spikes become broader because K+ channels stay open longer

rubric: Without voltage-gated Na+ channels the regenerative depolarization cannot occur, so propagation stops, while the resting potential is set mainly by K+ leak.
Distractors confuse Na+ channel block with demyelination or K+ channel effects.

items.prompt: A stroke damages the hand region of the left primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) but spares motor cortex. Which deficit do you predict?

options.label: Weakness of the right hand with normal touch
Loss of touch localization in the right hand
Loss of touch localization in the left hand
Loss of vision in the right visual field

rubric: Somatosensory pathways cross the midline, so left cortex represents the right hand, and sensory cortex damage impairs touch, not strength.
Distractors ignore the crossing or swap sensory and motor cortex.

items.prompt: In a brain slice, a postsynaptic neuron is voltage-clamped at -80 mV while a presynaptic input is stimulated with a high-frequency train that normally induces LTP. Glutamate is released normally and AMPA receptors work. What do you predict?

options.label: LTP occurs, since glutamate alone opens NMDA channels fully
LTP occurs, because hyperpolarization boosts Ca2+ entry
No LTP, because AMPA receptors cannot bind glutamate
No LTP, because Mg2+ still blocks NMDA channels

rubric: NMDA receptors need glutamate plus depolarization to expel Mg2+, so clamping at -80 mV prevents the Ca2+ entry needed for LTP.
Distractors treat glutamate binding as sufficient or reverse the effect of hyperpolarization.

items.prompt: Which treatments would be expected to increase serotonin signaling at synapses? Select all that apply.

options.label: An inhibitor of tryptophan hydroxylase
An MAO inhibitor that slows serotonin breakdown
A 5-HT receptor antagonist acting on postsynaptic cells
An SSRI that blocks the serotonin transporter

rubric: Blocking reuptake and slowing degradation both raise synaptic serotonin.
An antagonist blocks the receptors, and blocking tryptophan hydroxylase reduces serotonin synthesis.

items.prompt: In a patch-clamp experiment on a neuron, chloride's equilibrium potential is -70 mV. The cell is held at -40 mV, and a GABA-A receptor agonist is applied so that the channels open. What happens to chloride?

options.label: Cl- flows out of the cell, because the interior is more positive than outside
No net Cl- flow, because the channels pass current only at the resting potential
Cl- flows into the cell, driving Vm toward -70 mV
Cl- flows into the cell, because it is negatively charged, driving Vm toward 0 mV

rubric: At -40 mV the membrane is above E_Cl, so the driving force pushes Cl- inward and moves Vm toward -70 mV.
Distractors reverse the direction of the driving force or ignore the equilibrium potential.

items.prompt: A patient cannot recognize familiar faces, yet identifies the same people by their voices, reads fluently and sees fine detail normally. Which interpretation best fits this pattern?

options.label: Selective damage to ventral occipitotemporal face areas
Bilateral hippocampal damage that prevents forming any new memories of people
Damage to primary visual cortex that blocks much of the incoming visual input
Damage to Broca's area that impairs retrieving and producing people's names

rubric: Intact acuity, reading and voice recognition with failed face recognition points to a selective deficit in face-specialized ventral visual cortex.
Distractors invoke damage that would cause broader visual, language or memory problems.

items.prompt: A long stretch of an axon is demyelinated, and conduction fails there although the neuron is otherwise healthy. Which explanation best accounts for the failure?

options.label: Nodal Na+ channels are destroyed, so no node can ever fire again
Resting potential rises along the axon, inactivating every Na+ channel
Myelin loss blocks vesicle release at the terminal directly
Current leaks from the bare membrane, so the next node stays below threshold

rubric: Without insulation, current leaks out and capacitance increases, so the depolarization reaching the next node falls short of threshold.
Distractors attribute failure to channel destruction, resting potential or terminal release, none of which is the primary mechanism.

items.prompt: Patients with damage to region A fail task X but pass task Y. Patients with damage to region B pass task X but fail task Y. What is the best inference?

options.label: Regions A and B form one serial pathway for both tasks
Tasks X and Y rely at least partly on different regions
Task X is simply harder than task Y for all patients
Region A is necessary for all cognition tested here

rubric: A double dissociation indicates the two tasks depend at least partly on separable neural substrates.
Distractors ignore that the reversed pattern rules out a simple difficulty difference or a single shared pathway.

items.prompt: After a drug is applied, the EPSC evoked by a single stimulus rises by 50%, the paired-pulse ratio falls, and mEPSC amplitude is unchanged. Where does the drug most likely act?

options.label: Increased presynaptic release probability
Slower transmitter clearance from the cleft
Increased postsynaptic membrane capacitance
More postsynaptic AMPA receptors at each synapse

rubric: Higher release probability depletes vesicles faster, lowering the paired-pulse ratio, while the quantal size (mEPSC) is unchanged.
Postsynaptic or clearance changes would alter mEPSC amplitude rather than the paired-pulse ratio.

items.prompt: A study finds that BOLD signal in region R rises during a memory task, and a headline claims R is necessary for memory. What is the strongest objection?

options.label: Memory depends on several regions, so R cannot be needed by the task
Activation is correlational and doesn't show R is required for memory
BOLD mainly tracks inhibitory firing, so it says little about function
fMRI spatial resolution is too coarse to tie activity to a region

rubric: Imaging shows association; necessity needs causal tests such as lesions or inactivation.
Distractors misstate what BOLD measures or what fMRI can resolve.

items.prompt: Which findings together would point to a postsynaptic rather than presynaptic locus for LTP expression? Select all that apply.

options.label: Paired-pulse ratio decreases after induction
Presynaptic vesicle release probability rises
Paired-pulse ratio is unchanged after induction
mEPSC amplitude increases after induction

rubric: Larger quantal size with unchanged release properties indicates more or stronger postsynaptic receptors.
A falling paired-pulse ratio or higher release probability indicates a presynaptic change.

items.prompt: A researcher raises extracellular K+ from 4 mM to 12 mM while recording from a neuron. At first it fires rapidly, then it falls silent with its membrane potential sitting near -45 mV. Which mechanism best explains the silence?

options.label: Synaptic vesicles are depleted at the terminals, so the neuron can no longer release transmitter or spike
Chloride equilibrium shifts above threshold, so GABA-A channels open and strongly inhibit the cell
K+ channels close fully, so repolarization never completes and the membrane stays depolarized
Na+ channels inactivate during sustained depolarization, so spikes cannot be generated

rubric: Higher external K+ depolarizes the cell, and sustained depolarization inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels, a depolarization block.
Distractors point to K+ channel closure, chloride or vesicle depletion, which do not explain a silent depolarized cell.

items.prompt: A patient with multiple sclerosis (demyelinated axons) reports that her vision blurs after a hot shower and clears as she cools down. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.label: Warming shortens the action potential, so less current reaches a demyelinated stretch and it may fail to reach threshold
Warming raises the membrane capacitance of bare axon, so every node of Ranvier needs much more charge before it can reach threshold
Warming speeds K+ channel closing, so the axon stays depolarised after each spike and cannot fire again until it cools
Warming lowers Na+ channel density along the axon, so spikes can no longer be initiated at the axon hillock at all

rubric: Higher temperature speeds channel kinetics and shortens the spike, shrinking the safety factor in already compromised axons.
Distractors invent changes in capacitance, channel density or K+ closing that temperature does not produce.

items.prompt: In a voltage-clamp experiment on an axon, a step to 0 mV evokes an early inward current followed by a sustained outward current. After applying tetrodotoxin (TTX), only the outward current remains. What does this show?

options.label: The early inward current is carried by Ca2+ and the outward current by Cl-, because TTX blocks neither of those ions' channels
Both currents flow through one channel type, and TTX blocks only the fast inactivation gate of that one channel
The outward current is driven by the inward current, so TTX should have abolished both currents together
The inward current flows through voltage-gated Na+ channels; the outward current uses separate, mainly K+, channels

rubric: TTX selectively blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, so the surviving outward current must use other channels, mainly K+.
Distractors assume the wrong ions, a single channel type, or that the currents depend on each other.

items.prompt: After bilateral hippocampal damage, a patient improves daily at mirror-tracing but cannot recall ever doing the task. Which interpretation best fits this dissociation?

options.label: The patient has a retrieval deficit only, so both kinds of memory are stored normally but the hippocampal damage blocks access to the episode
Declarative memory formation requires the hippocampus, while skill learning relies on separate circuits such as basal ganglia and cerebellum
Procedural learning of the skill depends on the hippocampus, while recall of the episode relies on separate cortical areas that remain intact
The improvement shows that working memory is intact, and intact working memory alone is enough to build long-term motor skills over days

rubric: Intact skill learning with lost episodic recall indicates separable memory systems.
Distractors reverse the roles of the systems or wrongly equate the pattern with a retrieval-only or working-memory effect.

items.prompt: A drug applied to a brain slice lowers the frequency of miniature EPSCs without changing their amplitude, and raises the paired-pulse ratio of evoked EPSCs. Where is the most likely site of action?

options.label: Postsynaptic dendritic spines, which shrink so that fewer events are detected at the soma
Postsynaptic AMPA receptors, whose reduced conductance lowers each event while leaving release unchanged
Glial uptake, since faster transmitter clearance would reduce event size and the paired-pulse ratio
Presynaptic terminals, where release probability falls and so fewer vesicles fuse per spike

rubric: Lower mEPSC frequency with unchanged amplitude and a higher paired-pulse ratio indicate reduced presynaptic release probability.
Postsynaptic explanations would change amplitude, not frequency or paired-pulse ratio.

items.prompt: After an injury, a patient has loss of vibration and proprioception plus weakness in the right leg, and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg. Which lesion best explains this?

options.label: A left-sided lesion of the primary somatosensory cortex, with fibres crossing in the medulla
A complete transection at spinal level T10, which would abolish all sensation below it
A right-sided hemisection of the spinal cord, with ascending pain fibres crossing near entry
A lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere, where motor and sensory tracts cross twice

rubric: Brown-Séquard pattern: dorsal columns and corticospinal fibres are ipsilateral, while spinothalamic fibres cross at entry, so pain loss is contralateral.
A complete transection or cortical lesion would not give this crossed pattern.

items.prompt: A synapse on a distal dendrite produces a much smaller EPSP at the soma than an identical synapse near the soma. Which factors would make this decay worse? Select all that apply.

options.label: A thin dendrite, which gives high axial resistance along its length
Higher membrane resistance, which lengthens the space constant
A thicker dendrite, which lowers axial resistance and so lengthens the space constant
A dendrite with many open leak channels, which gives low membrane resistance

rubric: Decay worsens with a short length constant: leaky membrane (low Rm) and thin dendrites (high Ri).
Thicker dendrites and higher membrane resistance extend the length constant, so they reduce decay.

items.prompt: A researcher records from cortical neurons in tissue from an animal model of epilepsy. GABA-A inputs normally reverse at -75 mV, but in these neurons they reverse near -50 mV, and cells fire more readily when GABA is applied. Resting threshold is unchanged at -45 mV. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Reduced KCC2 activity raises intracellular Cl-, so GABA-A opening hyperpolarises less or even depolarises
Greater NMDA receptor block by Mg2+, which would make inhibitory currents reverse closer to threshold
Lost GABA-A receptors, which leaves a smaller conductance yet the same reversal potential for the remaining channels
Increased Na+/K+ pump activity lowers intracellular K+, shifting the GABA-A reversal potential upward

rubric: A shifted Cl- reversal potential points to altered chloride homeostasis, such as KCC2 downregulation.
Receptor number changes conductance, not reversal potential; the other distractors involve unrelated ions.

items.prompt: A lab needs to track the spiking of individual neurons in a freely moving mouse for several weeks. Criteria: millisecond resolution, single-cell isolation, stable chronic implant. Which method best meets these criteria?

options.label: PET imaging of glucose uptake, since it reports metabolic activity of cells over repeated sessions
Scalp EEG, since it records electrical activity continuously across weeks without surgery
Chronically implanted silicon probes or tetrode arrays recording extracellular spikes
Functional MRI, since it maps whole-brain activity with high spatial coverage in moving animals

rubric: Chronic extracellular probes give millisecond single-unit resolution in behaving animals.
EEG, fMRI and PET lack single-cell resolution or millisecond timing.

items.prompt: A fMRI study finds that region X activates strongly during a memory task, and the authors conclude that X is necessary for the task. Which critique is the strongest?

options.label: fMRI measures only neural spiking, so the claim could be settled by checking blood flow patterns
The sample is too small, and a larger fMRI study with more participants would then establish necessity directly
Activation is only correlational, so necessity needs a causal test like lesion or inactivation
Activation in one region implies that every other region is idle during the task, so the claim is overstated

rubric: Necessity is a causal claim that correlational imaging cannot establish.
Distractors misdescribe fMRI (blood oxygenation, not spiking) or suggest that more of the same data would fix the inference problem.

items.prompt: Blue light delivered to a brain region in mice expressing channelrhodopsin makes them turn left. Criterion: the conclusion must be that activating those neurons causes the turning. Which control matters most?

options.label: Delivering the same light in mice lacking the opsin, to rule out heat or visual effects of light
Recording from the same neurons after the experiment, to confirm that they fire during turning
Repeating the experiment in a different brain region, to show that turning is generally reflexive
Measuring the same turning in mice with identical opsin expression but delivering no light at all

rubric: Light delivered in opsin-negative animals separates opsin-driven effects from light, heat or visual artefacts.
No-light controls cannot reveal such artefacts, and the other options do not test causation.

items.prompt: A team wants to monitor hundreds of identified excitatory neurons in superficial cortex during a task. Criteria: many cells at once, genetic cell-type identity, millisecond spike timing is not required. Which approach is best?

options.label: Two-photon calcium imaging with a genetically encoded indicator expressed in the target cell type
Intracranial EEG over the cortex, which gives a population signal from the surface
Postmortem staining of immediate early genes, which marks activity without needing live recording
Whole-cell patch clamp from each neuron in turn, which gives the best temporal resolution

rubric: Two-photon imaging with genetic targeting meets the criteria of many identified cells and relaxed timing needs.
Patch clamp cannot cover hundreds of cells, EEG lacks cell identity, and staining is not live monitoring.

items.prompt: A knockout of gene G (absent from conception) gives mice with impaired spatial learning. Criterion: show that G is needed for learning itself, not just for development. Which design would be best?

options.label: Measure brain weight in knockouts, since normal weight would rule out developmental effects
Test the knockouts on a second maze, since a second task would settle the developmental question
Induce deletion of G in adult mice, then test learning, with controls given the same inducing treatment
Compare more knockout mice, since a larger sample would separate learning from development

rubric: An adult-inducible conditional knockout isolates the adult function of G from developmental effects.
More animals, more tasks or brain weight do not separate development from learning.

items.prompt: In monkeys, neurons in region Y fire more as the juice reward offered gets larger. The authors conclude that Y encodes subjective reward value. Which are valid criticisms of this conclusion? Select all that apply.

options.label: Single neurons cannot encode value, because only large populations can carry information
Value was not dissociated from reward size, for example by varying the animal's preferences or choice options
Firing correlated with reward size must be noise, since neurons never respond to quantities
Larger rewards may also raise arousal, licking or attention, which could drive the firing instead

rubric: Confounds such as arousal or motor activity, and the lack of a value-versus-size dissociation, weaken the inference.
The other two options are false general claims about neural coding.

items.prompt: A lab asks how a motor cortex area contributes to a lever press that lasts 2 seconds. Criteria: silence the area within milliseconds, reverse within seconds, and limit compensation by other circuits. Which approach is best?

options.label: Optogenetic inhibition during the press, since light-gated silencing is fast and reversible
Muscimol infusion, since it silences the area but takes minutes to act and hours to wear off
Surgical aspiration of the area, since permanent removal gives the cleanest test of its role
A constitutive knockout of a gene in the area, since it removes the area's function from birth

rubric: Optogenetic inhibition is fast and reversible, so it meets the timing and compensation criteria.
Lesions, muscimol and constitutive knockouts act too slowly, are not quickly reversible, or invite compensation.

items.prompt: A lab claims a drug 'enhances LTP' because field EPSP slope in CA1 rose 40% after tetanus. Judged against the criterion of showing a postsynaptic, NMDA-receptor-dependent mechanism, which critique is strongest?

options.label: Field recordings sample population activity, so the slope increase may reflect more fibers recruited rather than synaptic strengthening; whole-cell recordings would be needed before any LTP claim
Tetanic stimulation also recruits inhibitory interneurons, so the slope increase probably reflects altered presynaptic release rather than a postsynaptic NMDA-receptor-dependent change
Slope alone cannot separate presynaptic from postsynaptic changes, so without APV controls and paired-pulse or quantal analysis the mechanism is unsupported
A 40% rise is modest for CA1, and without a time-matched vehicle group showing stable baseline, the increase could be drift and not potentiation of the synapse

rubric: Mechanism claims need manipulations (APV) and measures (PPR, quantal analysis) that localize the change.
Distractors assert false thresholds or invalidate field recordings wholesale.

items.prompt: To test whether neurons in region X are necessary for a learned lever press, you need reversibility within one session and temporal precision of seconds. Which method best meets these criteria?

options.label: Post-hoc c-Fos mapping after training, because activity-dependent labeling shows which neurons are necessary for the behavior
Optogenetic inhibition, because it silences cells within seconds and reverses when the light stops
Chronic knockout of a gene enriched in X, because it removes the protein throughout development and gives stable effects
Electrolytic lesion of X, because permanent damage gives the cleanest and most complete loss of function across sessions

rubric: Optogenetic inhibition is reversible and temporally precise.
Lesions and knockouts are irreversible and allow compensation; c-Fos is correlational.

items.prompt: A paper reports that fMRI activity in the fusiform region predicts face recognition, concluding the region 'is the face module'. Which critique best weighs the evidence against the claim of necessity and specificity?

options.label: Face recognition engages many distributed regions, so the claim is weakened because a single region's activity cannot be shown to matter more than others
BOLD signal reflects blood flow rather than firing, so the correlation is weak evidence because hemodynamic measures only loosely track neural activity
The sample was large enough that almost any region would correlate with behavior, so the reported fusiform effect is likely a statistical artifact of power
Correlation cannot show necessity, and responses to expert non-face categories would challenge specificity, so lesion or stimulation data are needed

rubric: Necessity needs causal perturbation; specificity needs control categories.
Distractors overstate: BOLD does track neural activity; regional specialization can exist.

items.prompt: Two models explain a neuron's direction selectivity: (A) asymmetric inhibition delayed along the preferred-null axis, (B) dendritic nonlinear summation of sequential inputs. Which result most strongly favors A over B?

options.label: Selectivity is reduced when GABA-A receptors are blocked while excitatory inputs remain intact
Selectivity persists when the cell is hyperpolarized below spike threshold at the soma
Selectivity correlates with dendritic spine density measured in fixed tissue afterward
Selectivity is larger for slow motion than for fast motion across all tested stimuli

rubric: Loss of selectivity with inhibition blocked specifically implicates inhibitory asymmetry.
Other results are compatible with both models or merely correlational.

items.prompt: A single-unit study finds a motor cortex neuron fires most for rightward reach. Under a population-vector view versus a 'preferred-direction coding' view of single cells, which interpretation best fits the criterion of predicting reach from data?

options.label: Tuning curves are only artifacts of averaging across many trials, so decoding reach direction from single trials must fail
Direction is read from the weighted activity of many broadly tuned neurons, so prediction stays robust despite noisy cells
Broad tuning means each neuron carries no usable direction information, so decoding reach from such cells cannot work
Each neuron alone fully encodes reach direction, so the single best-tuned neuron should be chosen and the rest ignored

rubric: Population vectors pool broadly tuned cells for robustness.
Distractors assume single-cell sufficiency or no information.

items.prompt: A group claims that a hippocampal 'engram' cell ensemble stores a fear memory. Which findings would count as strong evidence for sufficiency and necessity combined? Select all that apply.

options.label: Tagged cells show higher c-Fos than random cells during training
Total hippocampal activity rises during any novel experience
Optogenetically reactivating tagged cells triggers freezing in a neutral context
Silencing the tagged cells during testing impairs recall of the fear memory

rubric: Artificial reactivation shows sufficiency; silencing shows necessity.
Elevated c-Fos and general activity are correlational.

items.prompt: A team records from a cortical neuron whose firing ramps before a decision. They propose it integrates evidence. A colleague notes the ramp also appears when the animal's choice is fixed in advance by a cue and no evidence is shown. Which judgment of the integration claim is best?

options.label: The claim is unaffected, because a ramp that appears in both conditions shows the neuron encodes the upcoming choice, which is what integration means
The claim is weakened, because ramping may reflect anticipation or motor preparation, so slope must vary with evidence strength
The claim is refuted, because a neuron that ramps without any evidence cannot also integrate evidence when evidence is present
The claim is confirmed, because a ramp before the response shows the neuron is accumulating information toward a decision bound

rubric: Integration predicts ramp slope scaling with evidence strength; a ramp without evidence suggests other causes.
Distractors over- or under-claim.

items.prompt: Design a test of whether dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error. Constraints: separate prediction from reward value, and include a case with a negative error. Which design fits?

options.label: Record during free feeding in hungry and then sated animals, and check that firing is higher when hungry because reward value is higher
Record during a cue-reward task, then omit the expected reward on some trials and check for a dip below baseline
Record while giving only rewards of increasing size across trials, and check that firing rises steadily with reward magnitude
Record while giving only unpredicted rewards at random times, and check that cells fire reliably at each reward delivery

rubric: Omission of a predicted reward isolates negative prediction error.
Other designs cannot separate prediction from value or lack a negative error.

items.prompt: You want to show a synapse's potentiation is expressed presynaptically with minimal perturbation of the postsynaptic cell. Which assembled protocol meets all constraints?

options.label: Whole-cell record with strong postsynaptic depolarization during induction, then compare EPSC amplitude and its coefficient of variation before and after
Apply an AMPA receptor antagonist throughout, then compare the field potential slope at matched stimulus intensities before and after induction
Delete postsynaptic NMDA receptors, then test whether basal transmission and induction of potentiation are both lost in the knockout
Record EPSCs with paired-pulse stimulation, then compare paired-pulse ratio and mEPSC frequency versus amplitude after induction

rubric: Paired-pulse ratio and mEPSC frequency changes indicate presynaptic expression.
Other options either cannot localize expression or abolish the response.

items.prompt: Propose an experiment to test that a cerebellar circuit learns a timed eyeblink response via climbing-fiber error signals. Constraints: causal, and distinguishing error signal from sensory cue. Which fits best?

options.label: Record Purkinje cell simple spikes during paired tone and puff training, and test whether their rate change tracks blink timing
Lesion the cerebellar cortex before tone-puff training, then check whether the animal fails to acquire the conditioned blink
Raise the tone volume across sessions while imaging cerebellar BOLD signal, and test whether the response scales with intensity
Pair tone with puff, then replace the puff with optogenetic climbing-fiber stimulation and test whether the blink develops

rubric: Replacing the unconditioned stimulus with climbing-fiber stimulation tests the teaching signal causally.
Other options are correlational or abolish the behavior without isolating the error signal.

items.prompt: Design a closed-loop epilepsy intervention meeting: detect seizure onset within 100 ms, act only during events, avoid chronic circuit alteration. Which is best?

options.label: Surgical removal of both hippocampi, ending seizure generation permanently in every patient
Daily systemic anticonvulsant at the maximum tolerated dose to keep neural excitability low
Continuous high-frequency stimulation of the focus at all times to prevent any seizure spread
Real-time EEG detection of ictal onset triggering brief focal stimulation, off otherwise

rubric: Closed-loop triggering satisfies detection speed, event-only action, and minimal chronic change.
Other options act continuously or irreversibly.

items.prompt: Build a computational model of a ring attractor for head direction. Which feature must the design include to hold a heading without input and update it on rotation?

options.label: Random fixed-weight recurrent connectivity that stores each heading as a separate stable fixed point, with no velocity input
Feedforward connections only, with per-cell thresholds tuned to each direction and a copy of the angular velocity signal added to every cell
Local recurrent excitation with broad inhibition, plus velocity-gated asymmetric input that shifts the bump
Uniform all-to-all excitation with global inhibition scaled to total activity, so a bump forms at a fixed location and is reset by each turn

rubric: Recurrent excitation with inhibition sustains a bump; asymmetric velocity input shifts it.
Other designs cannot persist or update.

items.prompt: Design a study to test whether a cortical area is needed for tactile discrimination, not just for movement of the response. Which elements must it include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A control task requiring the same response but no tactile judgment
Recording only from neurons already known to be tuned
Use of a single animal to reduce variability
Reversible inactivation of the area during the stimulus period

rubric: Reversible inactivation plus a motor-matched control separates perception from response.
Selective recording is correlational; one animal weakens inference.

items.prompt: A team plans to restore vision in retinal degeneration by expressing a light-sensitive channel in surviving retinal cells. Constraints: it must work at ambient light without external devices, it must not depend on the cell type being genetically defined by the disease, and it must preserve spatial resolution. Which design best meets them?

options.label: Express a highly light-sensitive opsin in surviving inner retinal neurons, such as bipolar or ganglion cells
Express a low-sensitivity opsin in ganglion cells and rely on bright goggles to deliver intense light to them
Express a light-gated channel in optic nerve glial cells so that the signal is carried along the whole nerve
Express a UV-only channel across the whole retina, because brightness does not matter for spatial resolution

rubric: Targeting surviving cells with a sensitive opsin and light amplification works under ambient light while keeping cell-level resolution.
Other options ignore sensitivity or the cell type needed.
